title: On the Impossibility of Robust Combiners for Cryptographic Groups
authors: Cong Zhang, Wenli Wang, Taiyu Wang, Hong-Sheng Zhou, Pengfei Chen, Zhihong Jia, Jian Liu, Jinfei Liu, Moti Yung, and Kui Ren
abstract:
A $(k,n)$-robust combiner for a primitive $\mathcal{P}$ combines $n$ candidate instantiations of $\mathcal{P}$ into a single scheme that remains secure as long as at least $k$ of them remain secure. Robust combiners have been extensively studied for primitives such as hash functions, public-key encryption, and oblivious transfer, but much less is known in the setting of cryptographic groups. In this work, we initiate the study of robust combiners for cryptographic groups in Maurer's generic group model (GGM), where algorithms access group elements only through abstract algebraic operations.

We ask whether one can combine $n$ candidate groups into a single group that remains secure provided that at least $k$ of the underlying groups remain secure. A natural baseline is the direct-product construction, which preserves search hardness but fails for decisional assumptions and incurs substantial representation overhead. We show that these limitations are in fact inherent.

Our first result is a complete impossibility for the decisional Diffie--Hellman assumption: for every polynomially bounded $n$ and $k$ with $k<n$, there is no generic $(k,n)$-robust combiner for cryptographic groups that preserves DDH security. Our second result gives a tight threshold for search assumptions in the regime where $n$ and $k$ are fixed constants. For the discrete logarithm problem, robust generic combination is possible when the combined group order is large enough to encode the secrets of $n-k+1$ components; concretely, if $\log N \ge (n-k+1)\lambda$, where the component groups have distinct $\lambda$-bit prime order, then a robust combiner exists. Conversely, if $\log N \le (n-k)\lambda$, then no generic $(k,n)$-robust DLog-secure combiner exists.

These results identify a fundamental limitation of robust hedging at the group level. Decisional assumptions such as DDH cannot be robustly combined in the GGM, while search assumptions admit robustness only at essentially optimal representation cost. Consequently, robustness for group-based cryptography must in general be achieved at higher layers, such as protocol design or key derivation.

1        Introduction
A basic principle of robust design is to avoid placing complete trust in any single component,
and cryptography is no exception. Robust combiners provide a principled way to hedge such
uncertainty: instead of committing to a single candidate instantiation of a primitive, one com-
bines several candidates into a single scheme that remains secure as long as sufficiently many of
the underlying candidates remain secure. This paradigm is especially appealing when the long-
term reliability of any individual assumption or implementation is unclear. Over the past two
decades, robust combiners have been extensively studied for a range of cryptographic primitives,
including hash functions [BB06, Pie07], public-key encryption [Her05, DK05], and oblivious trans-
fer [HKN+ 05, MPW07].
    Many cryptographic systems, however, are built not directly from such primitives, but from
cryptographic groups; see, for example, the extensive literature on group-based cryptography [DH76,
ElG84, CS03]. In particular, foundational hardness assumptions such as the discrete logarithm
problem (DLog), the computational Diffie–Hellman (CDH) assumption, and the decisional Diffie–
Hellman (DDH) assumption underlie a broad range of protocols and systems. This raises a natural
question: can robustness already be achieved at the level of the underlying group?
    A natural starting point is the direct-product construction. Given two cyclic groups G1 = ⟨g1 ⟩
and G2 = ⟨g2 ⟩ of orders p1 and p2 , respectively1 , one may form the product group G = G1 × G2
with componentwise operations and generator g = (g1 , g2 ). For search assumptions such as DLog
and CDH, this construction immediately provides a form of robustness: a DLog instance in the
product group has the form
                                     (g, g x ) = (g1 , g2 ), (g1x , g2x ) ,
                                                                         

and recovering x requires solving the corresponding search problem in each active coordinate.
Thus, direct products give a simple and natural baseline for robust group combination.
   At the same time, the direct-product construction already exposes two fundamental obstacles.
The first concerns decisional security. In the product group, a Diffie–Hellman tuple takes the form

                       (g, g x , g y , g xy ) = (g1 , g2 ), (g1x , g2x ), (g1y , g2y ), (g1xy , g2xy ) ,
                                                                                                      


whereas a random tuple takes the form

                                 (g, g x , g y , g z ) = (g1 , g2 ), (g1x , g2x ), (g1y , g2y ), (g1z , g2z ) .
                                                                                                             


The combined instance therefore exposes its full coordinatewise algebraic structure, rather than
hiding it inside a single group. As a result, once one component fails to preserve DDH security,
the direct product need not preserve DDH either. This leads to our first question:

          Can DDH-secure groups be robustly combined while retaining DDH security?

    The second obstacle is efficiency. Even when direct products preserve search hardness, they
do so at a substantial representational cost: if the component groups have orders p1 and p2 , then
the combined group has order p1 p2 , and each group element must carry both coordinates. Thus,
robustness is obtained only at the price of increased group size and representation overhead. This
leads to our second question:

          Can DLog-secure groups be robustly combined with substantially less overhead than the direct-
          product construction?

1.1    Our results
In this work, we answer both questions in the negative. Specifically, we formalize them within
Maurer’s generic group model [Mau05] and show that DDH-secure groups cannot be robustly
combined in a generic manner. By contrast, for DLog-secure groups, we show that robust combi-
nation is possible only above a tight threshold on the group order.
    We emphasize that studying these questions in the generic group model is particularly well
motivated. For many algebraic constructions, generic approaches are among the most natural
ones to consider, and they are often attractive from an efficiency perspective as well. Moreover,
identifying the exact boundary of what robust combiners can achieve in the generic setting is
not merely of theoretical interest; it may also have practical implications when choosing concrete
security parameters.
Impossibility of robust combiner for DDH (Section 4). As discussed above, the direct-product
construction cannot achieve DDH security: once a single underlying group fails to preserve DDH
security, this already suffices to reveal the distinguishing bit in the DDH game for the combined
group. We show that this is not merely a weakness of the direct-product approach, but a fun-
damental barrier in the DDH setting. In particular, we prove that robust generic combiners for
DDH-secure groups are impossible.

Theorem 1.1 (Informal). Let λ be the security parameter. Let k and n be any polynomials in λ with k < n.
Then there is no (k, n)-robust generic combiner for DDH-secure groups.

1.2    Technical overview
The framework. We prove our results in Maurer’s generic group model, which, together with
the incomparable model of Shoup [Sho97], constitutes one of the two main frameworks for for-
malizing generic-group computation. At a high level, in both models, algorithms are given oracle

                                                        4
access to the group operation and to an equality test for group elements. The key difference lies in
how oracle queries are specified.
    In Maurer’s model, an algorithm specifies a query by referring to group elements that have
already appeared during the computation, for example, by indicating the 3rd and the 5th previ-
ously generated elements. Moreover, group elements in Maurer’s model can only be manipulated
through the oracle interface, namely via group operations and equality tests. In Shoup’s model,
by contrast, group elements come with explicit random encodings, and queries are specified in
terms of those encodings. We refer the reader to Section 2.3 for a formal description of Maurer’s
generic group model.
    For ease of exposition, we focus in this section on the special case of a (1, 2)-robust generic
combiner for cryptographic groups. The relevant definitions and proof techniques extend to the
general (k, n) setting in a straightforward manner.

Robustness of generic combiners. Following [HKN+ 05], a robust combiner should remain secure
as long as sufficiently many of its candidate inputs remain secure. In the present setting, however,
the candidate inputs are themselves generic groups. This creates a modeling issue. Each generic
group is unconditionally hard against any adversary making only polynomially many generic
queries, so the standard notion of an efficient generic adversary is too weak to represent the idea
that one of the underlying candidates is already “broken.”
    To model corruption meaningfully, we therefore consider a stronger adversarial model. The
adversary is allowed to make an unbounded number of queries to exactly one of O1 and O2 ,
where the choice of the corrupted oracle is fixed in advance and is not made adaptively during
the attack.2 The remaining oracle is still accessed only polynomially many times, and so must
continue to satisfy the usual generic hardness guarantees.
    This is precisely the form needed in our lower bounds. If there exists an adversary that is
allowed unbounded access to one fixed oracle and nevertheless breaks the combined construc-
tion, then no (1, 2)-robust generic combiner can exist. Indeed, robustness would require a generic
reduction that turns such an attack into successful attacks on both underlying groups. But the re-
sulting reduction inherits unbounded access to at most one of the two groups. Consequently, one
of the two component groups would have to be broken using only polynomially many generic

1.3    Interpretation
Our results admit two complementary interpretations.
Practical perspective. Our results identify a fundamental limitation of what may be viewed as
algebraic hedging: one cannot, in general, obtain robustness for group-based cryptography by com-
bining multiple candidate groups within the group abstraction itself. Thus, if the goal is to hedge
against uncertainty in the underlying algebraic assumption, then robustness should instead be
sought at higher layers of the cryptographic stack—for example, through protocol-level design,
compiler transformations, or key-derivation mechanisms—rather than through the construction
of a universally robust combined group.
Theoretical perspective. Theoretically, our results reveal a sharp boundary for robust combina-
tion in algebraic settings. First, our work turns a long-standing folklore intuition into a formal
theorem: robust combiners for DDH-secure groups do not exist in the generic setting. Second, we
show that this impossibility is not merely a pathology of the model, but reflects a deeper divide
between decisional and search assumptions: DDH is generically non-combinable, whereas DLog
admits robust combination only above a tight order threshold. In this sense, our work uncovers a
qualitative asymmetry between decisional and search hardness in the robust-combiner regime for
groups.

2.1     Robust combiners
We follow the formulation of robust combiners for cryptographic primitives from [HKN+ 05]. We
begin by recalling the notion of a cryptographic primitive.

Definition 2.1 (Cryptographic Primitive [RTV04]). A primitive P is a pair ⟨F, R⟩, where F is a set of
functions f : {0, 1}∗ → {0, 1}∗ specifying correctness, and R is a relation on pairs ⟨f, A⟩, where f ∈ F
and A is an adversarial machine, specifying security.

      • Efficient implementation. A function f is an implementation of P if f ∈ F. An efficient
        implementation of P is an implementation that is computable in polynomial time.
      • Secure implementation. An adversarial machine A is said to P-break f if ⟨f, A⟩ ∈ R. An
        implementation f is secure if no PPT adversary A P-breaks f .

    An efficient implementation of P will also be called a candidate for P. A robust combiner takes
several candidates for the same primitive and outputs a single implementation that remains secure
as long as sufficiently many of the candidates are secure.

Definition 2.2 ((k, n)-Robust Combiner [HKN+ 05]). Let P be a cryptographic primitive. A (k, n)-
robust combiner for P is a PPTM C that takes n candidate implementations as input and implements P
while satisfying the following properties:

      • Robustness. If at least k of the input candidates securely implement P, then C also securely imple-
        ments P.



                                                        13
      • Efficiency. The running time of C is polynomial in the security parameter λ, in n, and in the input
        lengths of the primitive.
    The definition above allows trivial combiners that ignore the candidate implementations and
realize the primitive independently. Such constructions are usually uninformative, since their
security does not derive from the candidates themselves. To exclude this behavior, one often
requires the construction and its proof to be black-box.
Definition 2.3 (Black-Box Combiner [HKN+ 05]). A (k, n)-robust combiner is said to be black-box if
the following conditions hold:
      • Black-box implementation. The combiner is an oracle PPTM that accesses the candidate imple-
        mentations only via oracle calls to their implementation functions.
      • Black-box proof. For every candidate implementation, there exists an oracle PPTM R with oracle
        access to A such that if A breaks the combiner, then RA breaks at least n − k + 1 of the candidate
        implementations.

2.3     Generic groups and algorithms
In the setting of group-based cryptography, generic constructions are often the most natural place
to start: they capture what can be done using only the algebraic interface of the candidate groups,
without exploiting any accidental feature of a concrete encoding. Since our goal is to understand
whether robustness can already be achieved at the group layer, we focus on generic robustness,
namely the setting in which both the combiner and the reduction are required to be generic. We
formalize this using Maurer’s generic group model (GGM) [Mau05].

Definition 2.6 (Generic Group Model [Mau05]). Let N be a positive integer whose largest prime divisor
is a λ-bit prime. The generic group oracle O maintains a counter ctr ← 1 and an initially empty table B,
where each entry stores a value in ZN . Let Vi denote the value stored in the i-th entry. The oracle O provides
the following interfaces:

      • Labeling. On input x ∈ ZN , store x as Vctr , return ctr, and increment ctr.
      • Group operation. On input two integers i, j < ctr, store (Vi + Vj ) mod N as Vctr , return ctr, and
        increment ctr.
      • Equality test. On input two integers i, j < ctr, return 1 if Vi = Vj and 0 otherwise.

    A generic algorithm receives handles to group elements rather than their concrete representa-
tions. Formally, suppose A is given t group elements as input, say (g x1 , . . . , g xt ), together with an
optional auxiliary bit string. Instead of receiving explicit encodings of these group elements, A is
given their corresponding indices (X1 , . . . , Xt ) in the table B maintained by the relevant generic-
group oracle, where the first t entries of B store x1 , . . . , xt , respectively. The algorithm may then
access and manipulate these group elements only through queries to the oracle interface.
    We also allow different generic algorithms to exchange group elements during an interactive
computation. If an algorithm outputs k group elements, it outputs the indices of k entries in its
local table. When these values are passed to another generic algorithm, the recipient starts with a
fresh table whose first k entries contain the corresponding group elements.
    Finally, in our setting a generic algorithm may interact with multiple generic groups simulta-
neously. For generic-group oracles O1 , . . . , Om , each oracle maintains its own table and counter.
Indices produced by Oi refer only to entries in the table of Oi and cannot be used as inputs to
another oracle Oj for j ̸= i.

Remark 2.7 (DLog and DDH within the GGM). Within Maurer’s model, the DLog and DDH problems
are interpreted in the usual way, except that the adversary sees only handles. For DLog, the adversary is
given handles for g and g x and must recover x ∈ ZN . For DDH, the adversary is given handles for g, g x ,
g y , and either g xy or g z , and must distinguish the two cases. Here “efficient generic adversary” means an
adversary making only polynomially many oracle queries. Thus, the generic model isolates the algebraic
information that can be extracted from the oracle interface alone.

4    Impossibility of robust generic combiner for DDH
In this section, we prove the impossibility of robust generic combiners for DDH-secure groups.
Concretely, we construct an efficient generic adversary AI with respect to a set I ⊆ [n] satisfying
|I| = n − k such that, for any generic combiner C, the adversary AI breaks the DDH security of C.
    Moreover, it suffices to rule out the case of (n − 1, n)-robustness. Indeed, for any k ≤ n − 1, a
(k, n)-robust combiner is in particular also an (n − 1, n)-robust combiner. Hence, if no (n − 1, n)-
robust generic combiner exists, then no (k, n)-robust generic combiner can exist either. For clarity
of exposition, we begin with the special case n = 2, and then extend the argument to general n.
    In a nutshell, our adversarial strategy consists of three main steps:

    1. We first identify a suitable notion of partial information associated with a combined-group
       element. In particular, for a Diffie–Hellman label L(xy), we define a quantity P(xy) that
       captures a certain partial view of its representation.

    2. Next, we prove that this partial information P(xy) already suffices to distinguish L(xy) from
       a random label L(z) with high probability.
